rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 145–154 recall prohibitions in Abraham’s and Moses’ religions and refute the idolaters’ claim that God ordained their path and should redirect them if He disapproves.
rows.anchor: The things forbidden in the religion of Abraham (sws) and the religion of Moses (sws) are referred to.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 155–165 present the Qur’an’s conclusive communication; a prophet cannot produce a demanded sign, and the Prophet declares his guidance through Abraham’s religion.
rows.anchor: A prophet does not have the authority to show such a sign.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage invites anyone who wishes to follow the straight path, permits others to wander, and makes each person responsible before God for their deeds.
rows.anchor: Everyone is responsible before God for his deeds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The coming passage presents arguments for monotheism, the Hereafter, and prophethood through new styles and aspects.
rows.anchor: arguments in favour of monotheism, hereafter and prophethood are presented in some new styles with some new aspects.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’anic questions answered without waiting signal that the addressees cannot deny the answer; contrary beliefs or actions conflict with what they acknowledge.
rows.anchor: on such instances the addressees are no position to deny it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Answering immediately also shows that truth must be stated despite the addressees’ stubbornness.
rows.anchor: the truth must be told regardless of the stubbornness the addressees may show in response.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the Arabs practiced idolatry, they still acknowledged God as creator of the heavens and earth.
rows.anchor: the Arabs regarded God to be the creator of the heavens and the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s making mercy mandatory on Himself signifies the perfection of His mercy and guarantees that all its requirements will come to pass.
rows.anchor: signify the level of perfection in God’s mercy and also that whatever this attribute requires shall certainly come into being.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition in the gathering clause implies a suppressed verb meaning to drive someone.
rows.anchor: evidences the existence of a word that means “driving someone.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Judgement necessarily follows from divine mercy; without it the Creator would treat justice and injustice, virtue and vice, and good and evil as equal, leaving the world purposeless.
rows.anchor: The absence of such a day would mean that the creator of this universe is neither Most Gracious nor Ever-Merciful.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Day of Judgement chiefly fulfills mercy by rewarding the righteous; punishment of wrongdoers follows necessarily from that reward.
rows.anchor: the real purpose of the Day of Judgement is not to punish the wrongdoers; it is, in fact, to reward the righteous.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that only the self-lossful disbelieve in judgement is explained by verse 31.
rows.anchor: has been elucidated by verse 31 ahead.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording suppresses the contrasting expression for what moves during the day, paired with what is still at night.
rows.anchor: that is stationed) is suppressed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because God owns the heavens and earth and the audience accepts this, the Prophet should confront their worldly denial with the necessity of judgement; they will regret forgetting the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: he should ask them about the ownership of these heavens and the earth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night’s stillness and day’s activity are equally known to God, whose power and knowledge allow Him to gather everyone; verses 59–62 develop this theme.
rows.anchor: the darkness of night and the radiance of the day are equal with regard to His knowledge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since God owns and created everything, it is unfitting for the Prophet to take anyone else as guardian or protector, however much his audience dislikes this.
rows.anchor: it is not befitting for the Prophet (sws) to regard anyone else as his guardian and protector

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s giving nourishment while needing none expresses providence and mocks idols: only the creator and sustainer deserves protection, while idols depend on offerings and cannot create.
rows.anchor: The sentence “and He gives nourishment and is not nourished” is a reference to God’s providence, and also encompasses a subtle sarcasm for the Idolaters.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idolaters treat offered food as their deities’ favorite food, which they consume or enjoy by its aroma; offerings to God instead return to His poor creatures.
rows.anchor: the edibles the Idolaters presented to their deities would be regarded by them as their favourite food

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prophet first obeys the guidance he gives on God’s behalf, and his own compliance does not depend on whether people accept his invitation.
rows.anchor: a prophet is the first person to comply with the guidance he gives others on God’s behalf.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command not to become polytheists is an independent message the Prophet must convey; though addressed to him, its rebuke targets the audience under discussion.
rows.anchor: It is an independent statement that the Prophet (sws) must convey to them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who mistake worldly success for the real success will recognize their misery when the Day of Judgement arrives.
rows.anchor: forget the real success of the hereafter will realize their wretchedness when that day comes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No one can escape God’s grasp when He seizes them; verse 61 elaborates this control.
rows.anchor: There is absolutely no chance that anyone can escape His grasp when He will seize them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s wisdom and knowledge require a Day of Judgement, since without it the world would be purposeless.
rows.anchor: He brings about a Day of Judgement because without it, this world becomes a purposeless place.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s wisdom and knowledge require judgement, lest the world be purposeless, and rule out intercession that reverses good and evil.
rows.anchor: there is no possibility of any intercession that may turn good into evil and vice versa

rows.speaker: Most exegetes
rows.claim: Most exegetes coordinate “wa man balagh” with the accusative pronoun, meaning the Prophet warns his audience and those whom the Qur’an reaches.
rows.anchor: Most exegetes regard the expression i to be coordinated to the accusative pronoun

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author instead coordinates the expression with the nominative pronoun: those reached by the Qur’an should themselves warn others.
rows.anchor: However, I think this expression is coordinated to the nominative pronoun

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited Prophetic report tells those present to communicate the message to people absent, supporting the duty of recipients to warn others.
rows.anchor: let those present communicate this to those no present

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if the audience persists in assigning partners to God, the Prophet will not affirm their false testimony.
rows.anchor: if even after this, they think that God has partners, then the Prophet (sws) is not prepared to bear this false witness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet refuses to bear false witness for polytheism, declares God one, and disavows those associated with Him.
rows.anchor: He has been directed to proclaim that God is one and only and that he has acquitted himself from those they associate with God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The righteous among the People of the Book are meant; the pronoun “they recognize it” refers to the Qur’an, not the Prophet, because the verse addresses him directly.
rows.anchor: the righteous among the People of the Book are referred to here.

rows.speaker: Some people
rows.claim: Some exegetes take the recognition pronoun to refer to the Prophet; the author says the difference in purport is slight because Qur’an and Prophet mutually imply one another.
rows.anchor: Some people regard this pronoun to refer to the Prophet (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison to recognizing one’s sons depicts righteous People of the Book eagerly awaiting the Qur’an and Muhammad, like a father anticipating an estranged son’s arrival.
rows.anchor: in a similar way the righteous among the People of the Book were waiting or the Qur’ ān and Muḥammad (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s evidence was already known in earlier scriptures, awaited by the righteous among them; the self-lossful alone reject it and falsely accuse God.
rows.anchor: It is well-known and is mentioned in the previous scriptures.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This Makkan surah belongs to a phase when Madinan People of the Book were affected by it: pious readers saw scriptural prophecies fulfilled, while opponents stoked hostility; the passage encourages and warns respectively.
rows.anchor: it belongs to that Makkan phase in which the People of the Book in Madī nah had been impacted by it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The gathering includes all groups named earlier, all idolaters yet divided in their reasons for rejection, so each is addressed and warned according to its wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: each had different reasons to some extent for their rejection.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers reading fitna as the delusive trial of polytheism and false desires, which will be exposed when their supposed supports prove deceptive.
rows.anchor: I am more inclined to the first of these interpretations and have translated the verse accordingly.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative construes fitna as persecution of weak Muslims: the persecution ends and the persecutors suffer the calamities they inflicted.
rows.anchor: On the other hand, if this word is taken to mean persecution

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Either interpretation makes the verse’s sarcasm pronounced, with the exception understood as severed.
rows.anchor: in both cases the sarcasm would be steeped in the style of the verse and the exception would be regarded as severed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The imperative to look depicts a future scene; at judgement the polytheists first deny the very association for which they fought, echoing their earlier false testimony against God.
rows.anchor: The imperative verb “see” is to portray the situation so that a future event comes to mind.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their denial of polytheism at judgement reverses their earlier false witness against God in this world.
rows.anchor: in this world they bore false witness against God, as is mentioned in verse 19

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denials occur on separate occasions: first the idolaters call their deities, then deny polytheism when they see that calling them achieves nothing.
rows.anchor: At first they will call their deities and later when they will see that no headway is being made, they will deny

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heart’s cover and ear’s hardness are metaphors blocking understanding; these faculties define human life, and losing them leaves a person worse than an animal.
rows.anchor: The cover and hardness mentioned here are obviously metaphorical that stops and the heart and the ears to listen and understand.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This deprivation follows people’s own misdeeds: failing to use their faculties for their intended purpose results in their loss as divine punishment.
rows.anchor: This situation arises because of a person’s own misdeeds and is governed by a principle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A grammatically appropriate verb is suppressed in the clause about listening with the ears.
rows.anchor: A verb that is appropriate in meaning toۡۡۡن  collocating with ٰذن is suppressed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that they would not believe even if shown every kind of sign is literal in force: the whole universe is full of signs, but spiritual blindness defeats them; further miracles invite excuses, so they must listen to the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: The whole universe is replete with such signs but what is the cure for people who do not have eyes that can really see?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word asatir means an unfounded story.
rows.anchor: It means “an unfounded story.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’anic histories teach that nations rise and fall by moral principles: corrupt peoples are replaced by better ones, then tested in sovereignty; prophets serve as spiritual healers, and rejection brings destruction.
rows.anchor: This history shows that the rise and fall of nations are not accidental events.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an warns the Arabs through the destruction of earlier peoples that they face the same test with a messenger among them; they rejected the moral account of national rise and fall as natural aging.
rows.anchor: By narrating this history, the Qur’ ān has warned the Arabs that they too face a similar situation of life and death.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabs feared that rejecting the Prophet and Qur’an would bring punishment, so they called the Qur’an tales of the ancients; the author points to further detail at 16:24.
rows.anchor: they would say that this Qur’ān is a tale of the ancients which are being proclaimed by a madman.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the return-wish clause, an omitted verb meaning “we would affirm” answers their wish; the coordinated denial clause connects to that ellipsis, and the light imperfect expresses longing and confession.
rows.anchor: a very obvious answer to the desire was ﻓﻨﺼﺪق we attest) or a similar one.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage shifts from the fate of polytheist leaders in verses 21–24 to leaders who reject the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: Earlier in verses 21-24, the fate of the leaders of polytheism was described.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some wrongdoers listen to the Prophet to find points for polemics, not to understand; their misdeeds have sealed heart and ears, and even universal miracles will not persuade them.
rows.anchor: the purpose is to find some point of debate and dispute so that they can indulge in baseless polemics with him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their wish to return and believe is false: they knew the Prophet, Qur’an, reward, and punishment were truths, but worldly love, arrogance, and jealousy blinded them and they would deny again.
rows.anchor: They knew that the Prophet (sws) and the Qur’ān and reward and punishment are undeniable truths.
